title: Rapid tranquillisation and post-RT monitoring
blurb: Choose the NICE NG10 drug, know the legal basis, and monitor at the right frequency after rapid tranquillisation.
question: Kofi, 30, detained under section 3, was given IM lorazepam for rapid tranquillisation 20 minutes ago after de-escalation failed. He is now lying on his bed and appears to be asleep. How often should his physical observations be taken?

teach.body: NICE NG10 defines rapid tranquillisation (RT) as medication given by the parenteral route (usually intramuscular, exceptionally intravenous) when oral medication is not possible or appropriate and urgent sedation is needed. The MHA Code (26.94) uses a wider definition that includes oral medication, and says oral medication should always be considered before any injection, so name the source when you define RT. The aim is to calm, not to knock out: the Code says sedation should not stop the person understanding and responding (26.91). In plain English: RT is an emergency injection used when talking and oral medicine have failed and someone is at serious risk.

root.label: Choose IM medication
root.sub: Consider preferences, advance statements, health, pregnancy, intoxication, previous response

IM lorazepam OR IM haloperidol + IM promethazine

teach.caption: Children and young people: IM lorazepam, dose adjusted for age and weight (NG10 1.7.21).

NG10 next step

rows.label: Risk factors
values: Asleep or sedated, BNF max exceeded, drugs or alcohol, physical illness, harmed in restraint

rows.label: Checks
values: Pulse, BP, RR, temp, hydration, consciousness, side effects

teach.body: Restraint to give an IM injection to an unwilling patient needs legal authority: the MHA treatment rules for a detained patient, the MCA for someone lacking capacity, or another lawful basis. The Code is clear: RT must not be used to treat an informal patient who has capacity to refuse and has refused. RT must never substitute for adequate staffing, and the prescriber should state a preferred injection site that avoids prone restraint.

Wherever restrictive interventions might be used, resuscitation equipment must be immediately available: a defibrillator, bag valve mask, oxygen, cannulas, IV fluids, suction and first-line drugs, checked every week. Staff trained in immediate life support and a doctor able to use the equipment must be able to attend at once. When RT is being used, a senior doctor reviews all medication at least once a day.

Nurse Evans knows that 'appears asleep' is not reassuring after RT: it is one of the NG10 triggers for 15-minute monitoring. She records pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature, level of consciousness and hydration every 15 minutes, watching for respiratory depression from lorazepam, until there are no further concerns. She ensures he is observed within sight, and the incident is recorded and debriefed.

teach.text: Hourly is the minimum default, not the rule for everyone. A person who appears asleep or sedated, has taken drugs or alcohol, has a physical illness, was hurt in restraint or received more than the BNF maximum needs observations every 15 minutes. A sleeping patient is a reason to check more, not less.

items: NG10: RT = parenteral medication when oral is not possible or appropriate and urgent sedation is needed (the MHA Code also counts oral).
Adults: IM lorazepam alone, or IM haloperidol with IM promethazine.
Use lorazepam if no information, antipsychotic-naive, heart disease, long QT or no ECG.
Monitor at least hourly; every 15 minutes if asleep or sedated or another risk factor applies.
Needs legal authority; never for a capable informal patient who refuses, never for low staffing.

summary: You can now choose the NG10 drug for rapid tranquillisation, check the legal basis and set the right monitoring frequency. You know the safety equipment required and when to escalate.

A.q: Which medication does NICE NG10 recommend for rapid tranquillisation in an adult with no ECG available?
options: IM haloperidol with IM promethazine
IM haloperidol on its own
IM lorazepam on its own
IM promethazine on its own
A.why: NG10 1.4.39: if no ECG has been carried out, avoid IM haloperidol with promethazine and use IM lorazepam.

whyNot.0: This combination is avoided when no ECG has been done.
whyNot.1: Haloperidol alone is not an NG10 option and needs ECG caution.
whyNot.3: Promethazine alone is not an NG10 RT option.

A.q: After rapid tranquillisation, what is the minimum default frequency for physical monitoring when no risk factor is present?
options: Every 5 minutes
Every 15 minutes
At least hourly
Every 4 hours
A.why: NG10 1.4.45: monitor at least every hour until there are no further concerns; every 15 minutes if a listed risk factor applies.

whyNot.0: Five-minute checks are not the NG10 default.
whyNot.1: Fifteen-minute checks apply when a risk factor such as sedation is present.
whyNot.3: Four-hourly is too infrequent after RT.

A.q: Which observation set does NICE NG10 list for monitoring after rapid tranquillisation?
options: Pulse, BP, RR, temperature, hydration, consciousness
Pulse, BP, blood glucose, pupils, pain and weight
Pulse, BP, temperature, bowel chart, fluid balance
Pulse, RR, urine output, pain score and an ECG
A.why: NG10 1.4.45: monitor side effects and pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature, level of hydration and level of consciousness.

whyNot.1: Glucose, pupils, pain and weight are not the NG10 list.
whyNot.2: Bowel charts are not part of post-RT monitoring.
whyNot.3: This omits consciousness, temperature and BP from the NG10 list.

B.q: Zara, 26, is given IM haloperidol with IM promethazine. Thirty minutes later she has a partial response and remains highly agitated. What does NG10 suggest?
options: Give IM lorazepam at the same time
Consider a further dose of the same
Give IV diazepam for a faster effect
Wait 24 hours before any further dose
B.why: NG10 1.4.42: if there is a partial response to IM haloperidol with promethazine, consider a further dose.

whyNot.0: Lorazepam is considered after no response, not routinely added for a partial one.
whyNot.2: IV diazepam is not an NG10 RT option.
whyNot.3: NG10 allows a further dose after review; waiting 24 hours is not the guidance.

B.q: Paul, 50, has heart disease with a prolonged QT interval and needs rapid tranquillisation. Which is the most appropriate choice?
options: IM haloperidol with IM promethazine
Oral haloperidol crushed in a drink
IM haloperidol with an ECG afterwards
IM lorazepam on its own
B.why: NG10 1.4.39: with cardiovascular disease or a prolonged QT interval, avoid haloperidol with promethazine and use IM lorazepam.

whyNot.0: Haloperidol is avoided with a prolonged QT interval.
whyNot.1: Hiding medication in a drink is covert administration and haloperidol is still unsuitable.
whyNot.2: An ECG afterwards does not make haloperidol safe with known long QT.

B.q: Anna, 35, is an informal patient with capacity. She is shouting but not violent and refuses offered medication. A colleague suggests IM lorazepam. What is the correct position?
options: RT may be given as she is on a psychiatric ward
RT may be given under section 63 of the MHA
RT cannot be given as she is capable and refuses
RT may be given once two registered nurses agree
B.why: MHA Code 26.99: rapid tranquillisation must not be used to treat an informal patient who has capacity to refuse and has done so. Continue de-escalation and seek medical review.

whyNot.0: Being on a psychiatric ward gives no authority to treat without consent.
whyNot.1: Section 63 applies to detained patients, not informal ones.
whyNot.3: Nurses agreeing does not create legal authority.

C.q: Leon, 22, who had been drinking alcohol before admission, received IM lorazepam 15 minutes ago. He is awake, calm and talking. How often should his observations be taken?
options: Every 15 minutes, as he has taken alcohol
At least hourly, as he is awake and calm
Every 4 hours, as he is now settled
Once now, then on the next drug round
C.why: NG10 1.4.45: monitor every 15 minutes if the person has taken illicit drugs or alcohol, even if awake, until there are no further concerns.

whyNot.1: Hourly is the default, but alcohol is a listed risk factor.
whyNot.2: Four-hourly is too infrequent after RT.
whyNot.3: A single check does not meet NG10 monitoring.

C.q: Ruby, 40, received IM lorazepam with no response. She then had IM haloperidol with promethazine, also with no response, and remains a serious risk to others. What does NG10 advise next?
options: Give a third IM lorazepam dose straight away
Hold an urgent team review, second opinion
Add IM promethazine every 30 minutes
Exceed the BNF maximum dose to get control
C.why: NG10 1.4.43: if there is no response to haloperidol with promethazine and lorazepam has already been used, arrange an urgent team meeting to review and seek a second opinion if needed.

whyNot.0: Lorazepam has already failed; NG10 moves to urgent review.
whyNot.2: Promethazine alone is not an NG10 RT strategy.
whyNot.3: Exceeding the BNF maximum needs a planned, senior-led decision and triggers 15-minute monitoring; it is not the next step.

C.q: Two hours after RT, Dan, 28, is sleeping. On the 15-minute check his respiratory rate is 9 and he is hard to rouse. What should the nurse do first?
options: Let him sleep and recheck him in an hour
Document it and hand over to the next shift
Sit him upright and offer him oral fluids
Call for urgent help and support his airway
C.why: A low respiratory rate and reduced consciousness after RT suggest over-sedation and respiratory depression. Treat as an emergency: call for help, maintain the airway and use the resuscitation equipment NG10 requires to be immediately available.

whyNot.0: Reducing monitoring with signs of respiratory depression is dangerous.
whyNot.2: Oral fluids in a person who is hard to rouse risks aspiration.

reteach.title: Asleep means watch closer
reteach.question: How do you decide how often to monitor after RT?

blocks.h: Start from hourly, then ask five questions
blocks.body: Monitoring is at least hourly. Move to every 15 minutes if the person appears asleep or sedated, has had more than the BNF maximum, has taken drugs or alcohol, has a physical health problem, or was harmed during restraint. Continue until there are no further concerns.

blocks.text: A sleeping patient after RT is a 15-minute patient.

explain.body: IM lorazepam alone, or IM haloperidol with IM promethazine. Lorazepam if information is lacking, the person is antipsychotic-naive, or there is heart disease, prolonged QT or no ECG.

test.q: Mo, 19, has never taken an antipsychotic and needs rapid tranquillisation. Which medication should be used?
options: IM haloperidol with IM promethazine
IM lorazepam on its own
IM olanzapine with IM lorazepam
IM haloperidol on its own
test.why: NG10 1.4.38: if the person has not taken antipsychotic medication before, use IM lorazepam.

whyNot.2: This combination is not an NG10 option.
whyNot.3: Haloperidol alone is not an NG10 option.

explain.body: Write the initial RT prescription as a single dose and do not repeat it until the effect is reviewed. Check the total daily dose including regular, PRN and RT does not exceed the BNF maximum unless planned and senior-led.

test.q: How should the first dose of RT medication be prescribed, according to NG10?
options: As a regular dose given four times a day
As PRN with no maximum daily dose stated
As a single dose, reviewed before repeats
As a 3-day course to prevent relapse
test.why: NG10 1.4.44: write the initial prescription as a single dose and do not repeat it until the effect of the first dose has been reviewed.

whyNot.0: RT is not a regular treatment.
whyNot.1: PRN must have a stated maximum and RT starts as a single dose.
whyNot.3: RT is for immediate risk, not a course.

explain.body: Asleep or sedated; BNF maximum exceeded; illicit drugs or alcohol; pre-existing physical health problem; harmed during a restrictive intervention.

test.q: Which situation after RT requires observations every 15 minutes?
options: The person is calm and sitting talking
The person asks for something to eat
The person has been given a drink
The person appears to be asleep
test.why: NG10 1.4.45: monitor every 15 minutes if the person appears to be asleep or sedated.

whyNot.0: Calm and talking, with no other risk factor, needs at least hourly checks.
whyNot.1: Hunger is not an NG10 trigger.
whyNot.2: Having a drink is not an NG10 trigger.

explain.body: Needs legal authority (MHA treatment rules, MCA, or other). Never for a capable informal patient who refuses. Never a substitute for adequate staffing. Resuscitation kit immediately available and checked weekly.

test.q: How often should resuscitation equipment be checked where restrictive interventions might be used?
options: Every week
Every day
Every month
Every 6 months
test.why: NG10 1.4.3: resuscitation equipment must be immediately available, maintained and checked every week.

whyNot.1: NG10 specifies weekly, though local policy may add checks.
whyNot.2: Monthly is less often than NG10 requires.
whyNot.3: Six-monthly is far less often than NG10 requires.
